countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: People living together in an organized community, or an organized group formed for a shared purpose.
examples: American *society* has changed a lot in fifty years.
She belongs to a historical *society* downtown.
Several honor *societies* recruit students in the spring.

gloss: A group of people who live in the same place or share the same interests.
examples: The whole *community* turned out for the fundraiser.
Online *communities* can be surprisingly close-knit.
He grew up in a small farming *community*.

gloss: All the people living in a particular place.
examples: The town's *population* has doubled since 1990.
Rural *populations* are shrinking across the Midwest.
About a third of the *population* voted.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: An advanced, organized human society, or the condition of living in one.
examples: The Maya built one of the great *civilizations* of the Americas.
After a week in the woods, we were glad to get back to *civilization*.
Ancient *civilizations* left behind roads and temples.
contrast: Americans spell it *civilization*; the British write *civilisation*.

gloss: The human race as a whole, or the quality of being kind to others.
examples: A disease that threatens all of *humanity*.
She showed real *humanity* toward the refugees.
Crimes against *humanity* carry no statute of limitations.

gloss: A large, established organization such as a bank, a school, or a hospital.
examples: The university is the oldest *institution* in the state.
Financial *institutions* tightened their lending rules.
Marriage is an *institution* that keeps changing.
contrast: Americans say in-stih-TOO-shun; the British add a *y* sound: in-stih-TYOO-shun.

gloss: A system in which people or things are ranked one above another.
examples: The company has a strict *hierarchy*.
Wolves live in a clear social *hierarchy*.
She rose quickly through the *hierarchy*.
contrast: The *ch* is said like *k*, and the stress is on the first syllable: HY-uh-rar-kee.

gloss: A fixed social class that a person is born into and cannot leave.
examples: The *caste* system still shapes village life in parts of India.
Marriage between *castes* was once forbidden.
He was born into the lowest *caste*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *cast* (the actors in a play); only the spelling differs.

gloss: The small group of people with the most power, money, or skill.
examples: A tiny *elite* controls most of the wealth.
The country's political *elites* rarely agree.
He was never accepted by the local *elite*.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable, and *-ite* is said EET, not *eye-t*.

gloss: The highest social class, usually one with inherited titles and land.
examples: The French *aristocracy* lost everything in the revolution.
She married into the *aristocracy*.
European *aristocracies* have mostly faded away.

gloss: The people of the highest social rank, who hold inherited titles.
examples: The *nobility* paid almost no taxes.
He can trace his family back to the medieval *nobility*.
Members of the *nobility* were exempt from military service.

gloss: A poor farmer who works a small piece of land, especially in the past.
examples: Most *peasants* could not read or write.
The *peasant* families owned nothing but their tools.
He came from a *peasant* village in the mountains.
contrast: The *ea* is said EH, not EE: PEZ-uhnt.

gloss: A person who is legally owned by someone else and forced to work.
examples: Her ancestors were freed *slaves*.
The plantation was worked by *slaves*.
No one should be treated like a *slave*.

gloss: The practice of owning people and forcing them to work.
examples: *Slavery* was abolished in 1865.
The museum documents the history of *slavery*.
Modern *slavery* still exists in some industries.

gloss: A large group of families that claim a common ancestor.
examples: The Highland *clans* fought each other for centuries.
The whole *clan* shows up at Thanksgiving.
Rival *clans* controlled different valleys.

gloss: A small group inside a larger organization that disagrees with the rest.
examples: A *faction* of the party broke away.
Rival *factions* fought for control of the city.
The board split into two *factions*.

gloss: A small, closed group of friends who keep other people out.
examples: High school is full of *cliques*.
The department is run by a little *clique*.
She was never let into their *clique*.
contrast: Spelled with *-que* but usually said KLEEK; some Americans say KLIK.

gloss: An organized group of people who share an interest or a profession.
examples: The neighborhood *association* voted on the fence rules.
He joined the state bar *association*.
Several trade *associations* opposed the bill.

gloss: A group of teams, countries, or people joined together for a common purpose.
examples: Their town has its own bowling *league*.
The two nations formed a defensive *league*.
He plays in a recreational *league* on weekends.
contrast: The *u* is silent: LEEG.

gloss: A group of ordinary citizens who arm and organize themselves as soldiers.
examples: A local *militia* guarded the bridge.
Armed *militias* controlled the countryside.
He joined the state *militia* at seventeen.
contrast: The *t* is said like *sh*: muh-LISH-uh.

gloss: A small group of people working or playing together as a unit.
examples: A *squad* of police cleared the street.
She made the varsity *squad*.
Two bomb *squads* were called in.

gloss: An organized political group, or a group of people acting together.
examples: Neither *party* wanted an early election.
A search *party* went out at dawn.
Both *parties* signed the agreement.

gloss: A group of people who have come together in one place.
examples: It was a small family *gathering*.
Large *gatherings* were banned that spring.
A *gathering* of neighbors filled the church basement.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The state of belonging to a group, or a paid right to use something.
examples: *Membership* in the union is voluntary.
He let his gym *membership* lapse.
They sell family *memberships* at a discount.
contrast: Uncountable for belonging (*membership is voluntary*); countable for a subscription (*two memberships*).

gloss: The position of leading a group, or the ability to lead one well.
examples: The company needs stronger *leadership*.
Under her *leadership*, membership doubled.
He showed real *leadership* during the crisis.

gloss: A particular group of people defined by age, income, or similar traits.
examples: The show is aimed at a young *demographic*.
Advertisers track several *demographics* at once.
That *demographic* votes at very high rates.
contrast: The plural *demographics* also means the statistics about a population.

gloss: The ethnic group a person belongs to, based on shared origin and culture.
examples: The form asks about age, sex, and *ethnicity*.
Students of many *ethnicities* attend the school.
He never talks about his *ethnicity*.

gloss: A group of people seen as sharing physical features and ancestry.
examples: The law bans discrimination based on *race*.
People of all *races* live on this block.
*Race* is still a difficult subject in America.
contrast: The same word also means a speed contest: *a horse race*.

gloss: The state of being male or female, especially as a social role.
examples: The pay gap between *genders* is narrowing.
The survey does not ask about *gender*.
Both *genders* were represented on the panel.

gloss: Who a person is, or the qualities that make a group distinct.
examples: Language is a big part of national *identity*.
Someone stole his *identity* and opened three credit cards.
Teenagers try on different *identities*.

gloss: The presence of people of many different backgrounds in a group.
examples: The company talks a lot about *diversity*.
There is real *diversity* in this neighborhood.
*Diversity* on the board improved after the merger.

gloss: All the people born at about the same time.
examples: Her *generation* grew up without cell phones.
Three *generations* live under one roof.
The farm has been in the family for four *generations*.

gloss: A person born roughly between 1981 and 1996.
examples: *Millennials* are buying homes later than their parents did.
As a *millennial*, she barely remembers dial-up.
The ad campaign targets *millennials*.
contrast: Two *l*'s and two *n*'s — a word Americans misspell constantly.

gloss: A young person between childhood and adulthood.
examples: *Adolescents* need more sleep than adults do.
The clinic treats *adolescents* and young adults.
He was a moody *adolescent*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The time of being young, or a young person, usually a young man.
examples: He spent his *youth* on a farm in Iowa.
Two *youths* were questioned by police.
The program serves inner-city *youth*.
contrast: Uncountable for the time of life (*in my youth*); countable for a young man (*three youths*).

gloss: An older person in a family or community who is respected for it.
examples: The tribal *elders* met to decide.
Children here are taught to respect their *elders*.
A church *elder* opened the meeting.

gloss: A person who has stopped working because of age.
examples: Florida is full of *retirees*.
The plan covers current workers and *retirees*.
As a *retiree*, he volunteers three days a week.
contrast: Stress lands on the last syllable: rih-ty-REE.

gloss: A child who has just learned to walk, usually one to three years old.
examples: *Toddlers* get into everything.
She has a *toddler* and a newborn.
The class is for *toddlers* and their parents.

gloss: A very young child, especially one under a year old.
examples: The vaccine is safe for *infants*.
She was still an *infant* when they moved.
*Infants* sleep most of the day.

gloss: A baby that has just been born.
examples: The *newborn* weighed seven pounds.
*Newborns* need to eat every few hours.
They brought the *newborn* home on Sunday.
contrast: Americans say NOO-born; the British say NYOO-born.

gloss: A person who moves from one place to another to find work or a better life.
examples: *Migrants* pick most of the fruit in this valley.
The camp houses several hundred *migrants*.
He came here as a *migrant* worker in the eighties.

gloss: A person who leaves their own country to settle in another one.
examples: Thousands of *emigrants* sailed from that port.
Her grandfather was an Irish *emigrant*.
Letters from *emigrants* took months to arrive.
contrast: An *emigrant* leaves a country; an *immigrant* arrives in one — the same person, seen from opposite sides.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Being forced to live away from your own country, or a person living that way.
examples: The writer spent twenty years in *exile*.
Political *exiles* gathered in Paris.
He returned from *exile* to a hero's welcome.
contrast: Uncountable for the condition (*in exile*); countable for the person (*a group of exiles*).

gloss: A person from another country.
examples: *Foreigners* need a visa to work here.
He was the only *foreigner* in the room.
The law treats *foreigners* and citizens differently.
contrast: The *g* is silent: FOR-uh-nur.

gloss: A person born in a particular place, or one of its original inhabitants.
examples: She's a *native* of Cleveland.
The *natives* of the island fished for a living.
Ask a *native* — they'll know the shortcut.

gloss: A person who moves to a new region to live there permanently.
examples: The first *settlers* arrived by wagon.
*Settlers* cleared the land for farming.
A group of *settlers* built the town in 1851.

gloss: One of the first people to settle a place or to develop something new.
examples: *Pioneers* crossed the plains in covered wagons.
She was a *pioneer* in computer science.
The museum honors the town's *pioneers*.

gloss: A person who has recently arrived somewhere.
examples: The church runs a dinner for *newcomers*.
As a *newcomer*, he didn't know anyone.
*Newcomers* have pushed up the rents.

gloss: A person who does not belong to a particular group or place.
examples: In a small town you stay an *outsider* for years.
*Outsiders* aren't allowed at the meeting.
He ran for mayor as a political *outsider*.

gloss: A person who lives in the area, as opposed to a visitor.
examples: Ask the *locals* where to eat.
The bar is full of *locals* on Fridays.
A *local* pulled us out of the ditch.

gloss: The country where a person was born or where their people come from.
examples: He hasn't seen his *homeland* in thirty years.
Refugees dream of returning to their *homeland*.
The war drove them from their *homeland*.

gloss: All the people who live together in one house.
examples: The average *household* here has two cars.
Millions of *households* lost power.
She runs the whole *household* by herself.

gloss: A person's relatives, taken together.
examples: The hospital called his next of *kin*.
She has no *kin* left in the state.
They took the boy in as *kin*.
contrast: *Kin* never takes a plural *-s*, and it usually takes a plural verb: *his kin are farmers*.

gloss: A person from whom someone is descended, usually long ago.
examples: Her *ancestors* came over in 1848.
He traced his *ancestors* back six generations.
A distant *ancestor* fought in the Civil War.

gloss: A person who is related to someone who lived long ago.
examples: She's a direct *descendant* of the first mayor.
*Descendants* of the original settlers still farm here.
No *descendants* were left to claim the land.
contrast: Ends in *-ant*, not *-ent* — unlike *independent*.

gloss: A person with the legal right to receive property or a title when someone dies.
examples: She died without an *heir*.
The *heirs* fought over the farm for years.
He is the sole *heir* to the business.
contrast: The *h* is silent — *heir* sounds exactly like *air*.

gloss: A relative by marriage, such as a husband's mother or a wife's brother.
examples: We spend Christmas with my *in-laws*.
His *in-laws* live two blocks away.
She gets along with every *in-law* except one.
contrast: In the longer forms the plural goes on the first word: *brothers-in-law*, not *brother-in-laws*.

gloss: The son of your brother or sister.
examples: My *nephew* just started kindergarten.
She has four *nephews* and one niece.
He left the house to his *nephew*.
contrast: Americans say NEF-yoo; many British speakers say NEV-yoo.

gloss: The mother or father of one of your parents.
examples: Both of my *grandparents* were teachers.
The kids stay with their *grandparents* in July.
Every *grandparent* in the room was crying.

gloss: The child of your son or daughter.
examples: They have seven *grandchildren*.
Her first *grandchild* was born in May.
He reads to his *grandchildren* every Sunday.
contrast: Irregular plural: *grandchildren*, never *grandchilds*.

gloss: The woman married to your father who is not your own mother.
examples: His *stepmother* raised him from the age of six.
She's a great *stepmother* to those boys.
Fairy tales are full of wicked *stepmothers*.

gloss: A person who promises at a baptism to help raise a child.
examples: They asked my sister to be a *godparent*.
Both *godparents* came to the baptism.
His *godparents* still send him birthday cards.

gloss: An adult who is legally responsible for a child who is not their own.
examples: A court appointed his aunt as his *guardian*.
*Guardians* must sign the permission slip.
She became the *guardian* of her two nephews.

gloss: A person, usually a child, who relies on someone else for money and support.
examples: He claims two *dependents* on his taxes.
The insurance covers employees and their *dependents*.
She's listed as a *dependent* on her mother's return.
contrast: Americans spell the noun *dependent*; the British write *dependant* for the person.

gloss: A child whose parents have died.
examples: The war left thousands of *orphans*.
He was raised as an *orphan* by his uncle.
The charity places *orphans* with foster families.

gloss: A man whose wife has died.
examples: He's been a *widower* for ten years.
The club is mostly widows and *widowers*.
A quiet *widower* lives next door.

gloss: A man who has never been married.
examples: He stayed a *bachelor* until he was fifty.
The apartment looked like a *bachelor* lived there.
Two confirmed *bachelors* shared the house.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The legal union of two people, or the institution of being married.
examples: Their *marriage* lasted forty years.
*Marriage* rates have fallen since the nineties.
It was her second *marriage*.

gloss: The ceremony at which two people are married.
examples: The *wedding* is in a barn outside Austin.
We have three *weddings* this summer.
She cried through the whole *wedding*.

gloss: The legal ending of a marriage.
examples: Their *divorce* took two years.
*Divorces* are cheaper when nobody fights.
She filed for *divorce* in March.

gloss: An agreement between two people to marry.
examples: They announced their *engagement* at dinner.
The *engagement* lasted less than a year.
Both *engagements* were called off.

gloss: The person someone shares their life with, or someone who shares a business.
examples: She brought her *partner* to the office party.
The two *partners* split the profits evenly.
He introduced me to his *partner* of twelve years.

gloss: The way a child is raised and taught at home.
examples: He had a strict religious *upbringing*.
Their *upbringings* could not have been more different.
She credits her *upbringing* for her work ethic.

gloss: The time of a person's life when they are a child.
examples: She had a happy *childhood* in Ohio.
*Childhood* obesity is rising.
Their *childhoods* were spent on the water.

gloss: The period of a person's life after they have grown up.
examples: Most of his friendships date from early *adulthood*.
She reached *adulthood* before she was allowed to vote.
The disease usually appears in *adulthood*.

gloss: The state of being a mother.
examples: *Motherhood* changed her priorities.
She writes honestly about *motherhood*.
He never understood the demands of *motherhood*.

gloss: The legal act of taking another person's child into your family as your own.
examples: The *adoption* took eighteen months.
International *adoptions* have dropped sharply.
They're going through the *adoption* process now.

gloss: The legal right to care for a child, especially after a divorce.
examples: She was awarded *custody* of both kids.
They share joint *custody*.
The *custody* fight dragged on for years.

gloss: A person who looks after someone who is old, sick, or disabled.
examples: *Caregivers* rarely get a day off.
She became her father's full-time *caregiver*.
The program offers support for family *caregivers*.
contrast: Americans say *caregiver*; the British say *carer*.

gloss: A person paid to watch children while their parents are out.
examples: We couldn't find a *babysitter* on New Year's Eve.
Good *babysitters* get booked weeks ahead.
The *babysitter* arrived at seven.

gloss: A married woman whose main work is running her home.
examples: Her mother was a *housewife* all her life.
The show is about four suburban *housewives*.
She hated being called a *housewife*.
contrast: Irregular plural: *housewives*, with a *v*.

gloss: The relationship between people who are friends.
examples: Their *friendship* survived the move.
He formed lasting *friendships* in the army.
It started as a *friendship* and became more.

gloss: The way two people or groups behave toward each other, especially romantically.
examples: They've been in a *relationship* since college.
The *relationship* between the two towns is tense.
Long-distance *relationships* are hard.

gloss: Someone you know slightly but who is not a close friend.
examples: He's an *acquaintance* from the gym.
She invited a few *acquaintances* to the opening.
We're *acquaintances*, not friends.

gloss: A person who spends time with someone, especially on a trip or in daily life.
examples: The dog has been her *companion* for ten years.
He hired a *companion* for his elderly mother.
My travel *companions* were both from Texas.

gloss: A fellow member of a group, especially soldiers or political allies.
examples: He was buried beside his *comrades*.
Old *comrades* from the union came to the funeral.
She addressed the crowd as *comrades*.
contrast: Americans say KAHM-rad; the British say KOM-rayd.

gloss: A person of the same age or rank as someone else.
examples: Teenagers care most about their *peers*.
*Peer* pressure got him into trouble.
Her work is reviewed by *peers* before publication.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *pier*, a walkway out over water.

gloss: A friend, in casual American speech.
examples: He went fishing with his *buddies*.
My old army *buddy* called last night.
Hey, *buddy*, you dropped your wallet.

gloss: A person who is rejected by their community.
examples: After the trial he was a social *outcast*.
The village treated them as *outcasts*.
She writes about *outcasts* and loners.

gloss: An experienced person who advises and helps someone younger.
examples: Every new teacher is assigned a *mentor*.
He credits two *mentors* with his career.
She became a *mentor* to a dozen young lawyers.

gloss: A person or company that pays for or vouches for someone or something.
examples: The team lost its main *sponsor*.
New immigrants often need a *sponsor*.
Several *sponsors* pulled out of the festival.

gloss: Faithful support for a person, a group, or a country.
examples: *Loyalty* means a lot to him.
Her *loyalty* to the company never wavered.
*Loyalty* to the family came before everything.

gloss: Unity and mutual support among people who share a cause.
examples: The teachers marched in *solidarity* with the nurses.
There was little *solidarity* between the two unions.
They wore black as a show of *solidarity*.

gloss: The act of working together toward the same goal.
examples: The project needs *cooperation* from three agencies.
Thank you for your *cooperation*.
There was no *cooperation* between the departments.

gloss: A serious disagreement or fight between people or groups.
examples: The *conflict* between the neighbors lasted years.
Armed *conflicts* have displaced millions.
There's a *conflict* between what he says and what he does.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable (KAHN-flikt); the verb on the second (kuhn-FLIKT).

gloss: An argument or disagreement, especially a formal one.
examples: The *dispute* went to arbitration.
Border *disputes* have troubled the region for decades.
They settled the *dispute* out of court.

gloss: An agreement in which each side gives up part of what it wanted.
examples: They reached a *compromise* after six hours.
Marriage is full of small *compromises*.
Neither side would accept the *compromise*.

gloss: The power to affect how people think or act.
examples: She has a lot of *influence* on the board.
His teacher was a good *influence*.
Her early *influences* were all jazz musicians.

gloss: The general opinion people hold about someone or something.
examples: The school has an excellent *reputation*.
One bad review can ruin a *reputation*.
He built his *reputation* over thirty years.

gloss: The respect and admiration that a person or institution enjoys.
examples: The job carries a lot of *prestige* but little pay.
The award added to her *prestige*.
The university has lost some of its *prestige*.
contrast: Ends in the *zh* sound of *measure*: pres-TEEZH.

gloss: The respect a person earns by behaving decently.
examples: He was a man of *honor*.
They fought to defend the family's *honor*.
The park was named in *honor* of the fallen.
contrast: The *h* is silent (AH-nur), and Americans write *honor* where the British write *honour*.

gloss: The quality of deserving respect, and of behaving in a way that earns it.
examples: She faced the illness with *dignity*.
Every worker deserves to be treated with *dignity*.
He lost his job but kept his *dignity*.

gloss: Talk about other people's private lives, often unkind or untrue.
examples: The office runs on *gossip*.
I heard some *gossip* about the new manager.
Don't believe every piece of *gossip* you hear.
contrast: Uncountable — say *a piece of gossip*, not *a gossip*.

gloss: A story that spreads from person to person without being confirmed.
examples: *Rumors* of layoffs spread through the plant.
There's a *rumor* that the store is closing.
He denied the *rumor* on the record.
contrast: Americans write *rumor*; the British write *rumour*.

gloss: Friendly, generous treatment of guests.
examples: Southern *hospitality* is not a myth.
Thank you for your *hospitality* this weekend.
She works in the *hospitality* industry.

gloss: The set of rules for polite behavior in a society or a profession.
examples: Business *etiquette* differs from country to country.
It's a breach of *etiquette* to arrive early.
Nobody taught him basic table *etiquette*.
contrast: From French: most Americans say ET-ih-kut, though ET-ih-ket is also heard.

gloss: A custom or belief passed down within a family or a society.
examples: Fireworks on the Fourth are an American *tradition*.
The family has its own holiday *traditions*.
Every school here has a homecoming *tradition*.

gloss: A way of behaving that is usual among a particular group of people.
examples: Shaking hands is an old *custom*.
Local *customs* vary from valley to valley.
It is the *custom* here to bring a dish.
contrast: The plural *customs* also names the border office that inspects luggage.

gloss: The traditions, buildings, and culture handed down from earlier generations.
examples: She's proud of her Mexican *heritage*.
The town protects its architectural *heritage*.
Music is part of our national *heritage*.

gloss: A standard of behavior that is usual or expected in a group.
examples: Social *norms* change slowly.
Working from home has become the *norm*.
He ignored every *norm* of polite behavior.

gloss: An unfair difference between groups in wealth, rights, or opportunity.
examples: Income *inequality* has grown for decades.
The report lists *inequalities* in health care.
*Inequality* between the two districts is obvious.

gloss: An unfair act, or the condition of being treated unfairly.
examples: She spent her life fighting *injustice*.
The book lists the *injustices* of that era.
It would be an *injustice* to blame him.

gloss: Unfair treatment of people because of their race, sex, age, or beliefs.
examples: The suit alleges age *discrimination*.
*Discrimination* in hiring is illegal.
She faced *discrimination* at every job.
contrast: Uncountable — say *a lot of discrimination*, never *a discrimination* or *discriminations*.

gloss: An unfair opinion about someone formed before you know them.
examples: There's still a lot of *prejudice* against outsiders here.
He was raised without *prejudice*.
*Prejudice* dies hard in small towns.

gloss: The belief that one race is better than another, and unfair treatment based on it.
examples: The team was accused of *racism*.
*Racism* shaped where people were allowed to buy homes.
He spoke openly about the *racism* he faced.

gloss: Unfair treatment of people, usually women, because of their sex.
examples: *Sexism* in the industry is still common.
She called out the casual *sexism* in the meeting.
The policy was struck down as plain *sexism*.

gloss: An unfair preference for or against a person or group.
examples: The study controls for *bias*.
Everyone has *biases* they don't notice.
He showed a clear *bias* toward his own students.

gloss: A fixed, oversimplified idea about what people of a certain group are like.
examples: The movie leans on tired *stereotypes*.
She doesn't fit the *stereotype* at all.
*Stereotypes* about the South annoy him.

gloss: The forced separation of groups of people, especially by race.
examples: *Segregation* in schools was ruled unconstitutional.
He grew up under legal *segregation*.
Housing *segregation* persists in many cities.

gloss: The process of bringing separated groups together as equals.
examples: *Integration* of the schools took years.
The city has a long history of racial *integration*.
*Integration* into a new country is never easy.

gloss: Work aimed at bringing about political or social change.
examples: Her *activism* started in college.
Online *activism* rarely changes laws by itself.
He gave up law for full-time *activism*.

gloss: The giving of money and effort to help other people.
examples: He turned to *philanthropy* after selling the company.
American *philanthropy* funds many museums.
Her *philanthropy* focused on rural schools.
contrast: *Ph* is said like *f*, and the stress falls on the second syllable: fuh-LAN-thruh-pee.

gloss: The condition of having no job, or the number of people without one.
examples: *Unemployment* fell to four percent.
He's been collecting *unemployment* since March.
Youth *unemployment* is the real problem.

gloss: The condition of having nowhere to live.
examples: The city declared an emergency over *homelessness*.
*Homelessness* rose sharply after the rents went up.
Nobody has solved *homelessness* here.

gloss: The change in a poor neighborhood as wealthier people move in and prices rise.
examples: *Gentrification* pushed most of the old families out.
The new coffee shops are a sign of *gentrification*.
Residents organized against *gentrification*.

gloss: A small group of houses and buildings in the countryside, smaller than a town.
examples: She was born in a fishing *village*.
The road connects six *villages*.
The whole *village* came to the funeral.

gloss: A place with houses, stores, and streets, larger than a village but smaller than a city.
examples: He grew up in a small *town* in Kansas.
Both *towns* share a high school.
The *town* voted to build a new library.

gloss: A large, important town where many people live and work.
examples: New York is the biggest *city* in the country.
Several *cities* passed the same ordinance.
She moved to the *city* right after graduation.

gloss: A residential area on the edge of a city.
examples: They live in a quiet *suburb* of Chicago.
The *suburbs* grew fastest in the fifties.
It's a forty-minute drive from the *suburb* into town.

gloss: A part of a town or city where people live.
examples: It's a safe *neighborhood* with good schools.
The two *neighborhoods* are separated by the highway.
Everyone in the *neighborhood* knows him.
contrast: The *gh* is silent, and Americans write *neighborhood* where the British write *neighbourhood*.

gloss: A crowded, poor part of a city where the housing is bad.
examples: He grew up in the *slums* of the East Side.
The city cleared the *slum* in the sixties.
Millions still live in urban *slums*.

gloss: A self-governing district of a large city or state.
examples: Brooklyn is the most populous *borough*.
All five *boroughs* voted the same way.
The *borough* runs its own sanitation department.
contrast: Sounds like *burrow*, an animal's hole: BUR-oh. British speakers say BUH-ruh.

gloss: A person who owns the house they live in.
examples: *Homeowners* pay the property tax.
As a new *homeowner*, she's always fixing something.
The storm left thousands of *homeowners* without insurance.

gloss: All the people who work for a company or in a country.
examples: The company cut its *workforce* by a third.
Women entered the *workforce* in huge numbers.
Both *workforces* were unionized.

gloss: Work, especially hard physical work, or the workers who do it.
examples: The price includes parts and *labor*.
Organized *labor* backed the candidate.
Farms here depend on seasonal *labor*.
contrast: Americans write *labor*; the British write *labour*.

gloss: The job or profession a person does for a living.
examples: Write your *occupation* on the form.
Nursing is one of the fastest-growing *occupations*.
His *occupation* is listed as carpenter.

gloss: A young person learning a trade by working under a skilled worker.
examples: He started as an *apprentice* electrician.
The shop takes two *apprentices* a year.
*Apprentices* earn less while they train.

gloss: A person who is not a member of the military or the police.
examples: Hundreds of *civilians* were evacuated.
As a *civilian*, he missed the routine.
The base is closed to *civilians*.

gloss: A building where people convicted of crimes are locked up.
examples: He spent six years in *prison*.
The state closed two *prisons* last year.
She visits him in *prison* every month.
contrast: No article when you mean serving a sentence: *in prison*, not *in the prison*.

gloss: Something unpleasant done to someone because they broke a rule or a law.
examples: The *punishment* seemed too harsh.
Corporal *punishment* is banned in most schools.
Different states impose different *punishments*.

gloss: A person who is being kept in a prison or a similar institution.
examples: The prison holds two thousand *inmates*.
An *inmate* filed the complaint.
*Inmates* work in the laundry for pennies.

gloss: A person who fights against a government or refuses to obey authority.
examples: The *rebels* took the northern province.
He was a *rebel* even in grade school.
Government forces pushed the *rebels* back.
contrast: The noun is REB-ul; the verb *to rebel* is rih-BEL, stressed on the second syllable.

gloss: The ideas and tastes shared by most people in a society.
examples: The band never broke into the *mainstream*.
Those views are now part of the *mainstream*.
*Mainstream* opinion has shifted a lot.

gloss: A famous person, especially in entertainment or sports.
examples: Three *celebrities* showed up for the benefit.
He became a minor *celebrity* overnight.
*Celebrities* get treated differently everywhere.

gloss: The state of being known by many people.
examples: *Fame* came late in his career.
She never wanted *fame*, only the work.
The book brought him worldwide *fame*.

gloss: One person, considered separately from a group.
examples: The law protects the rights of the *individual*.
Several *individuals* were named in the report.
He's a strange *individual*, but harmless.

gloss: Human beings in general, or a nation sharing a language and culture.
examples: A lot of *people* showed up.
The indigenous *peoples* of the Northwest fished for salmon.
They are a proud *people* with a long history.
contrast: *People* is the everyday plural of *person*; the form *peoples* means nations or ethnic groups.

gloss: A home where children without parents are raised.
examples: She was adopted from an *orphanage* at four.
The state closed its last *orphanages* in the seventies.
He grew up in a church *orphanage*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Protection from weather or danger, or a building that provides it.
examples: The family took *shelter* in the basement.
The city runs three homeless *shelters*.
We adopted a dog from the *shelter*.
contrast: Uncountable as protection (*to take shelter*); countable as a building (*two shelters*).

ru: ясли, детский сад; присмотр за детьми
gloss: Care provided during the day for young children while their parents work.
examples: Both kids are in *daycare* now.
*Daycare* costs more than her rent.
The company opened a *daycare* center on site.
contrast: Americans say *daycare*; the British say *nursery*.

gloss: A public celebration or series of events, often held every year.
examples: The town holds a strawberry *festival* in June.
Both *festivals* were rained out.
She played at a folk *festival* in Colorado.

gloss: A public procession of people marching or riding through the streets.
examples: The Thanksgiving *parade* starts at nine.
Three *parades* were canceled for the storm.
Kids lined the street to watch the *parade*.

gloss: A social event where people who have not met in a long time come together.
examples: Our twentieth high school *reunion* is next fall.
Family *reunions* fill the campground every July.
He skipped the *reunion* on purpose.

ru: мероприятие по сбору средств; сборщик пожертвований
gloss: An event held to collect money for a cause, or a person who organizes one.
examples: The school held a bake sale as a *fundraiser*.
She's the campaign's top *fundraiser*.
Two *fundraisers* are scheduled for October.

gloss: An informal name used instead of a person's real name.
examples: His *nickname* in the army was Ace.
Every kid on the team has a *nickname*.
She hates both of her *nicknames*.

gloss: A family name, shared by parents and children.
examples: Her *surname* is hard to spell.
Both *surnames* appear on the birth certificate.
He kept his mother's *surname*.
contrast: Americans more often say *last name*; *surname* shows up mostly on forms.
